svg.title: ED-01 Step 9 revised sequence diagram
svg.desc: Revised treatment of ED-01 Step 9: ED-01 terminates after the assignment is sent but retains ownership of the acknowledgement timer, with crew acknowledgement and begin-response shown as an asynchronous continuation handled by AC-02, and a timeout branch escalating back to the dispatcher.
svg.text: ED-01 STEP 9 — Crew Acknowledges and Begins Responding
"Out of scope" is the right call for the behaviour. It is the wrong call for the timer.
ED-01 ENDS HERE — success guarantee: DispatchRecord exists, status ASSIGNED, assignment delivered to the crew device. Everything below is a continuation, not a step.
ref AC-02 — Acknowledge Dispatch and Respond (separate use case, separate diagram)
9.2 acknowledgeDispatch(dispatchId) — enters through the boundary, as the dispatcher's actions do
second clause — "begins responding" is a separate transition, minutes may pass
[ no acknowledgement within T ] — AC-02 never runs, so nothing inside AC-02 can detect this
→ re-alert, or return to STEP 2 to reassign. This branch is ED-01's, because ED-01 is the only use case still running.
1 The document contradicts itself. Step 9 is numbered in the main flow of the Dispatch Ambulance use case, but the sequence diagram annotates it "out of scope for ED-01." A step cannot be
both. Pick one: either delete it from the numbered flow and restate it as a post-condition, or realize it. The narrative currently promises nine steps and the diagram delivers eight.
2 You cannot delegate the timeout to a use case that never runs. This is the substantive point. If the crew never acknowledges, AC-02 does not execute — so no logic inside AC-02 can notice.
The watcher has to live in the use case that is still active, which is ED-01. Arming the timer is the last thing ED-01 does; cancelling it is the first thing AC-02 does. That single obligation is
what keeps a delivered-but-ignored assignment from sitting silently while a patient waits, and it is the piece that "out of scope" currently loses.
3 ref implies waiting. An interaction-use inside a sequence flow means "this happens here," so as drawn, ED-01's control flow blocks until the crew presses acknowledge. Nothing should
block on that. Show AC-02 as an asynchronous continuation past ED-01's end line, not as an inline step.
4 AmbulanceCrew is an actor with methods the system calls. Your spec gives it acknowledgeDispatch(dispatchId) and beginResponse(dispatchId), while Emergency Dispatcher — the other
human actor — has no methods at all. Actors invoke the system through a boundary; they are not invoked. The crew's actions should enter via AmbulanceCrewWorkspace exactly as the
dispatcher's enter via DispatchWorkspace. Keep AmbulanceCrew as the entity that records who is staffing the unit.
5 Two clauses, two transitions. "Acknowledges" and "begins responding" are separate events that can be minutes apart, and EMS response-time reporting depends on telling them apart —
ASSIGNED to ACKNOWLEDGED is a crew-alerting metric, ACKNOWLEDGED to IN_PROGRESS with the unit at EN_ROUTE is a turnout-time metric. One combined message would collapse both.
6 Your class spec is already equipped for all of this: recordAcknowledgement(), isAcknowledged(), getAcknowledgedAt(), Ambulance.acknowledgeDispatch(), Ambulance.beginResponse(),
and AmbulanceCallCenter.recordAcknowledgement(dispatchId, acknowledgedAt). None of them are reachable from any ED-01 message today.

Recommendation: renumber the use case to eight steps, add a post-condition and an acknowledgement-timeout guarantee, and keep AC-02 as the continuation. That removes the contradiction without pulling crew behaviour into ED-01.
